Both of my parents were drug addicts, and for most of my childhood, we were homeless. School wasn’t consistent—we moved constantly, and survival was the priority, not education. My dad was a career criminal, stealing whatever he could to support his addiction. Most of the food we ate was stolen. The cars we drove—and often slept in—were stolen. More than once, we watched from a distance as the police towed away everything we had. That kind of life forces you to grow up fast. At 13 years old, my dad was arrested again for GTA with priors and sentenced to 10 years, serving 7. My mom was still deep in addiction and mostly absent. Around that time, I managed to 10 11 rent a room on Motel Drive in Fresno, California. I looked older than I was, and no one questioned it. 7. Grit Grit is the ability to keep going when things are hard, uncertain, or not going your way. Strong leaders don’t rely on motivation—they rely on their willingness to push through discomfort, setbacks, and failure. Grit means showing up every day with the same intensity, regardless of how you feel or what obstacles are in front of you. It’s the diﬀerence between people who quit when things get tough and those who keep going until they win. Over time, grit becomes one of the biggest factors in long-term success because it allows you to outlast and outperform others. Example: After losing everything in 2008 and being $2 million in debt, I went back to the same dealership where I started, sold 28 cars my first month and started my journey back. Losing everything you worked for and starting over is extremely stressful but my grit would not allow me to fail. My hunger was greater, the chip on my shoulder was bigger. I felt like something was stolen from me and I had to get it back. I heard a quote once: “ Your ability to handle stress & pressure is your ceiling to success. ” 8. If the value exceeds the price, it’s a good deal. When the price is lower than the value, it’s a good deal. If you just want to turn a unit and don’t care about making money, just lower the price until you have gone below what the customer feels the value is.
